description: A hands-on water course from the U.S. Geological Survey's Water Science School. Your children follow water through the water cycle, discover why it is so unusual (surface tension, capillary action, density), then explore rivers, floods, groundwater, sinkholes, and water quality. Each lesson is one short USGS page to read online plus a kitchen or backyard experiment and a few questions. The Water Science School is a free, public-domain U.S. Government resource.
includes: Link to the exact Water Science School page for every lesson
A simple experiment or field task in every lesson
Rain gauge, aquifer model and solar still projects
Questions with answers for every lesson

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Evaporation
steps: Read Evaporation and the Water Cycle
Set two identical cups of water out, one in the sun and one in the shade; mark the levels and check each day this week
Draw the water cycle and add an evaporation arrow from the ocean

links.label: Read Evaporation and the Water Cycle

questions: What does evaporation turn liquid water into?
Where does most of the moisture in the atmosphere come from?
What happens to most of the water that evaporates from the oceans?
answers: Water vapor (a gas)
Oceans, seas, lakes and rivers (about 90 percent)
It falls back into the oceans as precipitation

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Condensation
steps: Read Condensation and the Water Cycle
Fill a glass with ice water on a warm day and watch the outside; explain where the drops came from
List three places you have seen condensation at home

links.label: Read Condensation and the Water Cycle

questions: What is condensation the opposite of?
Why is condensation so important to the water cycle?
answers: Evaporation
It forms clouds, which can produce precipitation

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Precipitation
steps: Read Precipitation and the Water Cycle
Set up a rain gauge (a straight-sided jar with a ruler) and record rainfall this month
Work out: how many gallons fall when 2 inches of rain land on one acre?

links.label: Read Precipitation and the Water Cycle

questions: What do tiny cloud droplets need in order to start growing into raindrops?
How many gallons fall when 1 inch of rain lands on one acre?
Why does most cloud water never fall as rain?
answers: A tiny particle of dust, salt or smoke to condense on
27,154 gallons
The droplets are too small to fall against the updrafts holding the cloud up

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Sublimation
steps: Read Sublimation and the Water Cycle
Put an ice cube in the freezer on a plate and check it over several days, or hang a wet cloth outside on a freezing day
Define sublimation and deposition in your notebook

links.label: Read Sublimation and the Water Cycle

questions: What is sublimation?
What is the opposite of sublimation called, and what is one example?
Name two conditions that help sublimation happen.
answers: A solid changing straight to a gas without melting first
Deposition, such as frost or snowflakes forming
Any two: low humidity, dry winds, high altitude (low air pressure), strong sunlight

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Evapotranspiration
steps: Read Evapotranspiration and the Water Cycle
Tie a clear plastic bag around a leafy branch on a sunny day and check it after a few hours
Label the three steps of transpiration on a plant drawing

links.label: Read Evapotranspiration and the Water Cycle

questions: What two processes make up evapotranspiration?
Through what tiny openings do leaves release water vapor?
answers: Evaporation and transpiration
Stomata

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Infiltration
steps: Read Infiltration and the Water Cycle
Pour the same cup of water on bare soil, grass, and pavement and time how fast it soaks in
List the factors that change how much water soaks into the ground

links.label: Read Infiltration and the Water Cycle

questions: Where can water go after it infiltrates the ground?
What is the biggest factor controlling infiltration?
answers: It can stay in the soil, move sideways, or sink deeper to recharge aquifers
The amount and type of precipitation (intensity and duration)

lessons.title: Lesson 7: Surface Runoff
steps: Read Surface Runoff and the Water Cycle
In the rain (or with a hose), follow where water flows from your roof or driveway
Make a list of impervious surfaces around your home

links.label: Read Surface Runoff and the Water Cycle

questions: What is surface runoff?
What is an impervious surface? Give two examples.
answers: Precipitation that flows over the land instead of soaking in
A surface water cannot pass through, such as roofs, roads, driveways or parking lots

lessons.title: Lesson 8: Ice, Snow, and Glaciers
steps: Read Ice, Snow, and Glaciers and the Water Cycle
On a world map, color Antarctica and Greenland and label how much of Earth's ice each holds
Press a cup of snow or crushed ice firmly and see how it turns harder and icier

links.label: Read Ice, Snow, and Glaciers and the Water Cycle

questions: Where is almost 90 percent of Earth's ice?
How does snow turn into glacier ice?
answers: Antarctica
Snow piles up year after year and its weight compresses it into ice

lessons.title: Lesson 9: Oceans: The Great Storehouse
steps: Read Oceans and Seas and the Water Cycle
Fill a 1-liter bottle as 'all Earth's water' and pour out about 3 percent to show fresh water
Taste-free test: dissolve salt in water and let it evaporate in a dish to see what stays behind

links.label: Read Oceans and Seas and the Water Cycle

questions: About what percent of Earth's water is in the oceans?
How much lower were the oceans in the last ice age?
answers: About 96.5 percent
About 400 feet lower

lessons.title: Lesson 10: Groundwater Storage
steps: Read Groundwater Storage and the Water Cycle
Fill a clear cup with gravel, add water, and point out the water table
Finish your water-cycle poster with every part from this unit

links.label: Read Groundwater Storage and the Water Cycle

questions: What is the top of the saturated zone called?
About what share of Earth's fresh water is groundwater?
answers: The water table
About 30 percent

units.title: Unit 2: The Amazing Properties of Water

lessons.title: Lesson 11: Facts About Water
steps: Read Facts About Water
Weigh a gallon jug of water on a bathroom scale and compare with the number on the page
Write down three water facts that surprised you
questions: About how much does a gallon of water weigh?
What is the pH of pure water?
Is 'wetness' one of our five senses?
answers: About 8.3 pounds
7 (neutral)
No; we mostly feel the water's temperature and movement

lessons.title: Lesson 12: The Universal Solvent
steps: Read Water, the Universal Solvent
Stir salt, sugar, sand, and oil into separate cups of water and record which dissolve
Draw a water molecule and mark its positive and negative sides
questions: Why is water called the 'universal solvent'?
What about a water molecule makes it good at dissolving things?
answers: It dissolves more substances than any other liquid
It is polar: one side is slightly positive and the other slightly negative

lessons.title: Lesson 13: Surface Tension
steps: Read Surface Tension and Water
Float a paper clip on water using a bit of tissue, then add a drop of dish soap and watch
Count how many drops of water fit on a coin before it spills
questions: What causes surface tension?
How do water striders stay on top of water?
answers: Water molecules at the surface cling strongly to each other (cohesion)
They use surface tension plus long, water-repelling legs that spread out their weight

lessons.title: Lesson 14: Adhesion and Cohesion
steps: Read Adhesion and Cohesion
Watch drops on wax paper and on a paper towel and decide which shows cohesion and which shows adhesion
Make a memory card: cohesion = water to water, adhesion = water to other things
questions: What is cohesion?
What is adhesion?
answers: Water being attracted to water
Water being attracted to other substances

lessons.title: Lesson 15: Capillary Action
steps: Read Capillary Action and Water
Stand a celery stalk or white flower in colored water overnight and look at it the next day
Dip a strip of paper towel into water and time how high it climbs
questions: What three forces work together in capillary action?
Why does water climb higher in a thin tube than a wide one?
answers: Adhesion, cohesion and surface tension
A thin tube has more inside surface for its size, so adhesion pulls water higher

lessons.title: Lesson 16: Water Density
steps: Read Water Density
Put an ice cube in water and in cooking oil, and float an egg in plain water and then in very salty water
Explain why ice floating matters for fish in a frozen pond
questions: What is density?
Why do ice cubes float?
At what temperature is water densest?
answers: The mass (weight) for a given volume
Ice is less dense than liquid water
About 4 °C (39.2 °F)

lessons.title: Lesson 17: Specific Heat
steps: Read Specific Heat Capacity and Water
Set a cup of water and a cup of sand in the sun for an hour and compare their temperatures
Explain why towns by the sea have milder weather

links.label: Read Specific Heat Capacity and Water

questions: What does it mean that water has a high specific heat?
Name one use of water that depends on its high specific heat.
answers: It takes a lot of heat energy to raise its temperature
Cooling, such as in a car radiator or in industry

lessons.title: Lesson 18: pH and Water
steps: Read pH and Water
Make red-cabbage indicator and test vinegar, baking-soda water, tap water, and lemon juice
Put each result on a 0–14 pH line
questions: What does a pH of 7 mean? Less than 7? More than 7?
Can vegetable oil have a pH? Why or why not?
answers: Neutral; acidic; basic
No; only water-based (aqueous) solutions have a pH

lessons.title: Lesson 19: How Much Does a Cloud Weigh?
steps: Read How Much Does a Cloud Weigh?
Follow the page's math step by step with a calculator
Explain why something so heavy can float

links.label: Read How Much Does a Cloud Weigh?

questions: About how much do the water droplets in the page's sample cumulus cloud weigh?
Why does the cloud float?
answers: About 1.1 million pounds (500,000 kilograms)
The cloud is less dense than the drier air below it

lessons.title: Lesson 20: Watersheds
steps: Read Watersheds and Drainage Basins
Crumple a sheet of paper, open it, color the ridges with marker, and spray it with water to see the 'watersheds'
Find which large river your home's watershed drains to
questions: What is a watershed?
What are the ridges between two watersheds called?
answers: All the land that drains water to a common outlet
The drainage divide

lessons.title: Lesson 21: Rivers, Streams, and Creeks
steps: Read Rivers, Streams, and Creeks
Visit a creek or look at one on a map and trace it from source to mouth
List where river water comes from besides rain running off the land
questions: Name two sources of the water in a river.
Name two ways runoff can be 'lost' before reaching a river.
answers: Runoff from the land and groundwater seeping in along the banks and bed
Any two: evaporation, use by plants (transpiration), use by people, animals drinking

lessons.title: Lesson 22: How Streamflow Is Measured
steps: Read How Streamflow Is Measured
Measure a small stream or gutter: time a floating leaf over 10 feet and estimate width and depth
Find a USGS streamgage near you on the online water-data map
questions: What is stream stage?
What are the three steps USGS uses to compute streamflow?
Where and when did USGS start its first streamgage?
answers: The height of the water surface (gage height)
Measure stage, make discharge measurements, and build the stage-discharge relation
On the Rio Grande in New Mexico, in 1889

lessons.title: Lesson 23: Floods and the '100-Year Flood'
steps: Read Floods and Recurrence Intervals
Roll a 100-sided die (or draw from 100 numbered slips) for 'years' to see that a 1-in-100 event can happen twice in a row
Explain the term '100-year flood' in your own words
questions: What is the chance of a '100-year flood' happening in any given year?
Does a 100-year flood this year mean the next one is 100 years away?
answers: 1 percent (a 1 in 100 chance each year)
No; the chance is the same 1 in 100 every year

lessons.title: Lesson 24: Impervious Surfaces and Flooding
steps: Read Impervious Surfaces and Flooding
Pour water on a tilted cookie sheet and on a tilted tray of soil; catch and compare what runs off
Suggest two ways a town could reduce runoff
questions: Why does paving land make floods worse?
Why was the house near Peachtree Creek raised 10 feet?
answers: Rain can't soak in, so it runs quickly into sewers and creeks
The creek flooded its first floor in 1975 and 1976

lessons.title: Lesson 25: Lakes and Reservoirs
steps: Read Lakes and Reservoirs
Find Lake Baikal, the Great Lakes, and Lake Mead on a map
Explain the difference between a natural lake and a reservoir
questions: How does a lake form?
What is the world's oldest, largest, and deepest freshwater lake?
answers: Water flows into a low spot faster than it can leave by outflow, seepage or evaporation
Lake Baikal in Siberia

lessons.title: Lesson 26: Hydroelectric Power
steps: Read Hydroelectric Power: How It Works
Build a pinwheel and turn it with water poured from a pitcher
Draw the path of water through a dam: reservoir, intake, turbine, generator

links.label: Read Hydroelectric Power: How It Works

questions: What turns the turbine in a hydroelectric plant? In a coal plant?
What does the turbine turn to make electricity?
answers: Falling water; steam from water heated by burning coal
A shaft in an electric generator

lessons.title: Lesson 27: What Is Groundwater?
steps: Read Groundwater: What Is Groundwater?
Dig a hole in damp sand (or at the beach) until water seeps in
Draw the unsaturated zone, saturated zone, and water table
questions: How does the amount of fresh groundwater compare with all the water in rivers and freshwater lakes?
What kinds of rock layers can slow groundwater down?
answers: There is about a hundred times more fresh water in the ground
Dense or tight layers such as granite or shale

lessons.title: Lesson 28: Aquifers
steps: Read Aquifers and Groundwater
Build an aquifer in a clear container with clay, sand and gravel layers, then 'rain' on it
Explain porosity and permeability with a sponge and a rock
questions: What is an aquifer?
Why does the hole at the beach fill with water?
answers: Rock or sediment underground that holds and gives up usable amounts of water
The sand is below the water table, in the zone of saturation

lessons.title: Lesson 29: Wells
steps: Read Groundwater Wells
Push a straw into your aquifer model and draw water out with a dropper
Label well casing, screen, and cap on a drawing
questions: Why do people in deserts depend on wells?
What does a well cap do?
Name the three kinds of wells the page describes.
answers: Surface water is scarce there, so groundwater is the main supply
Keeps out debris, insects and small animals
Dug, driven, and drilled wells

lessons.title: Lesson 30: Artesian Water
steps: Read Artesian Water and Artesian Wells
Model it: fill a bendy straw or tubing held high on one end and lower the other end to see water rise
Explain why a deep well is not always an artesian well

links.label: Read Artesian Water and Artesian Wells

questions: What makes water in an artesian well rise?
Where does the word 'artesian' come from?
answers: Pressure in a confined aquifer between poorly permeable layers
The town of Artois in France

lessons.title: Lesson 31: Sinkholes
steps: Read Sinkholes
Model a sinkhole: bury a sugar cube under damp sand and drip water on it
Find whether your state has limestone or other karst rock
questions: In what kinds of rock are sinkholes common?
Why did over 110 sinkholes form near Dover, Florida, in January 2010?
answers: Rocks groundwater can dissolve, such as limestone, carbonate rock and salt beds
Farmers pumped so much groundwater to protect crops from freezing that water levels dropped to record lows

lessons.title: Lesson 32: Land Subsidence
steps: Read Land Subsidence
Squeeze water out of a wet sponge stuffed in a cup and watch it shrink
Look at the photo of the pole near Mendota, California, and estimate how far the ground sank
questions: What causes most land subsidence in the United States?
Why does the ground sink when water is pumped out?
answers: Pumping too much groundwater (more than 80 percent of identified subsidence)
The water helped hold up the sediments, so they compact

lessons.title: Lesson 33: When Groundwater Runs Low
steps: Read Groundwater Decline and Depletion
Use two straws in one cup to show two neighbors' wells drawing down the same water
Write three ways a family can save water
questions: What is groundwater depletion?
About what share of people in the United States get drinking water from groundwater?
answers: Long-term falling water levels from pumping faster than recharge
About half (and nearly all rural people)

units.title: Unit 5: Water Quality and Water Use

lessons.title: Lesson 34: Turbidity
steps: Read Turbidity and Water
Make a simple 'Secchi' test: lower a white lid into jars of clear and muddy water and see when it disappears
List what makes water turbid
questions: What is turbidity?
Why are rivers usually more turbid after a rainstorm?
answers: How cloudy or clear water is, measured by how much light is scattered
Rain washes soil particles in, and faster flows stir up sediment

lessons.title: Lesson 35: Dissolved Oxygen
steps: Read Dissolved Oxygen and Water
Compare a still cup of water with one you stir hard and discuss which would get more oxygen
Explain why fish might struggle in a warm, still pond
questions: What does dissolved oxygen measure?
Below what level is water called hypoxic?
answers: How much oxygen is dissolved in water for living things to use
Less than 2 milligrams per liter

lessons.title: Lesson 36: Acid Rain
steps: Read Acid Rain and Water
Drop a piece of chalk or limestone in vinegar and in water and compare
Find the northeastern states on a map and explain why acid rain was worst there
questions: What is the usual pH of normal rain, and of acid rain?
Which gases help make rain acidic?
answers: Normal rain is a bit less than 6; acid rain is about 5.0–5.5 or lower
Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides
lessons.notes: The page calls acid rain a success story because regulations reduced it.

lessons.title: Lesson 37: How Much Is a Million Gallons?
steps: Read A Million Gallons of Water: How Much Is It?
Mark out 267 feet in a park or field to see the length of a million-gallon pool
Calculate how many 40-gallon baths are in a million gallons

links.label: Read A Million Gallons of Water

questions: How big a pool would hold a million gallons?
How many 40-gallon baths make a million gallons?
About how much does a million gallons of water weigh?
answers: About 267 feet long, 50 feet wide and 10 feet deep
About 8,340,000 pounds

lessons.title: Lesson 38: Desalination
steps: Read Desalination
Make a solar still: a bowl of salty water, a cup in the middle, plastic wrap, and a pebble on top; leave it in the sun
List places in the world that need desalination
questions: How salty is ocean water?
Name two ways to remove salt from water.
answers: About 35,000 parts per million
Distillation (boiling and condensing the steam) and reverse osmosis, shown in the page's plant photo

lessons.title: Lesson 39: The Story of Water in Dryville
steps: Read The Story of Water in Dryville
As you read, list every way the new town needs water
Draw a map of your own Dryville showing its water source, water treatment, and wastewater

links.label: Read The Story of Water in Dryville

questions: What is the first water need in a new town?
Name two possible sources of water for Dryville.
answers: Drinking water (a water source)
Any two: the creek or pond, a reservoir behind a dam, a well into the water table
lessons.notes: The page also offers a class-play script adapted by a Wisconsin teacher; that script is not a USGS work and is not used here.
